claim: Emphasis/pharyngealisation spread is trigger-specific rather than governed by one uniform domain: /ḍ/ can spread leftward across high /y/, while leftward spread from /ṭ/ is blocked by /y/ in the examined forms.

source_forms.transparent_for_d: aḅyaḍ 'white' (emphasis from /ḍ/ affects first syllable across /y/)
source_forms.opaque_for_t: yxayyəṭ 'he saws' (final /ṭ/ does not spread beyond the adjacent vowel)

normalized_environment: /y/ TRANSPARENT to LEFTWARD_SPREAD from /ḍ/ but OPAQUE to LEFTWARD_SPREAD from /ṭ/
scope: leftward emphasis spread inside phonological word
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The same segment /y/ has opposite transparency depending on the emphatic trigger, so a global 'y blocks emphasis' generalization is false.

claim: Rightward emphasis from /ṭ/ can extend across the entire phonological word, as shown by the lowered F2 of the final syllable in ṭṭəyybi 'you.FS cook'.
normalized_environment: RIGHTWARD [RTR] SPREAD from /ṭ/ may extend to RIGHT_EDGE(PHONOLOGICAL_WORD)
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The grammar's overall conclusion is explicitly asymmetric and cautious: not every emphatic consonant has the same spread potential.

claim: Inflectional prefixes remain outside the emphasis-spread domain in the examined Jewish Gabes forms even though they are part of the phonological word.
normalized_environment: LEFTWARD [RTR] SPREAD does not enter INFLECTIONAL_PREFIX
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The author treats the finding as based on the examples examined rather than as a universal theorem; related Palestinian Arabic shows prefix/suffix asymmetries of its own.

claim: The author's recordings do not support leftward emphasis spread across a boundary between morphologically independent words, contrary to an earlier report by Yoda.

no_crossword_spread: kifāš ḍáṛbu? 'how did he hit him?'

normalized_environment: LEFTWARD [RTR] SPREAD blocked by MORPHOLOGICAL_WORD_BOUNDARY in examined data
exceptions_or_counterexamples: This directly conflicts with Yoda 2006, who reported cross-word emphaticisation in the same example types; the disagreement is preserved rather than resolved by fiat.
section: discussion of sibilants and emphasis spread

claim: Rightward emphasis can affect the negative suffix /-š/, yielding emphatic [ṣ]; the author also reports that uvular /x/ can trigger this rightward emphaticisation in the negative particle.

source_forms.emphatic_trigger: mā ṣaḷḷáṣ 'he did not pray' (< negative /-š/)

normalized_environment: NEGATIVE_SUFFIX /-š/ -> [ṣ] under RIGHTWARD EMPHASIS; /x/ can act as trigger
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The rightward suffix effect contrasts with the lack of leftward cross-word spread in the same author's data, demonstrating directional and domain asymmetry.
